![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094658/assets/c0df23ec47d729f597c02acff1530dd646a6f6c506a6497a8cb4d75b7fce5e74.png)

As $i$ runs over $I,$ these line segments sweep the following rectangle that represents the union ${⋃}_{i\in I}{S}_{i}:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094658/assets/97a74b119ddb8a618d6564bc077d03a5a4ceb7152702beb3682f2eab1a436b70.png)

Therefore, in our case, the associated homogeneous equation is

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-{y}^{′}+3y=0.
$$

- The first system is not an initial value problem. It contains an equation only. No conditions are specified.

- The second system is not an initial value problem. It consists of a differential equation together with two conditions at different points in the domain of $y(x)$ (i.e., at $x=1$ and $x=2$). This is a **boundary value problem.**

- The third system is an initial value problem. The differential equation is together with two conditions at the same location in the domain of $y(x)$ (i.e., at $x=1$).
Therefore, we conclude that $u$ does *not* lie on the plane $Π.$

Since we found a solution $s=3,\,t=2,$ we conclude that $u$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
u=3b+2c.
$$

Finally, $s\cdot t=3\cdot 2=6.$
